questions.question: Will any U.S. state formally adopt a pause on new data-center construction by January 31, 2027?
questions.why_it_matters: A state-level pause could delay or prevent data-center projects and therefore constrain the infrastructure buildout that supports demand for NVIDIA systems. This policy outcome could occur independently of the hyperscalers’ reported capital-spending totals: spending plans could remain unchanged even if projects face a construction pause.
questions.why_not_already_covered: The existing questions track hyperscaler spending and compute-capacity additions, not whether a government formally pauses new data-center construction. The article describes political support for a pause, not an enacted policy; adoption would be a distinct policy outcome that could affect project timing or feasibility even if spending forecasts do not change.
questions.how_and_when_to_check: Check by January 31, 2027, an analyst’s check date at NVIDIA’s current fiscal-year end; the article does not state a deadline for any policy action. Review state legislation, executive orders, official state announcements, and other government records for a formally adopted pause. The article does not identify a particular state or pending measure.

evidence.quote: Lee flagged one more risk. Opposition to new data centers is turning into an election issue, and some Republican governors now back a pause.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article identifies a political development that could lead to a pause on new data-center construction. It does not say that any governor or government has formally adopted one.
evidence.original_speaker: The journalist; the article attributes the risk observation to Tom Lee.

evidence.what_it_shows: This provides the scale of NVIDIA’s current business and near-term revenue outlook, illustrating why a policy risk to data-center buildout could matter. It does not establish that a construction pause has been adopted or quantify its effect.

evidence.quote: Jay Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners holds the only sell rating on the stock. He argues the sold-out supply constraint caps the upside, because Nvidia cannot ship chips it has already promised.
evidence.what_it_shows: This is a countervailing consideration: near-term shipments are described as constrained by already-promised supply, which could limit how immediately a data-center pause affects deliveries. It does not resolve whether a government adopts a pause or its longer-term effect on demand.

But several governors reportedly back a pause and state representatives are reported to be implementing moratoriums. Those signals make at least one formal state pause by the January 31, 2027 check date more likely than none, so the forecast crosses to Yes (rung 1). The reports are not state-specific or confirmation of adoption, so this remains a forecast rather than an established outcome; the shipment constraint concerns near-term chip deliveries, not whether a state acts.
judgements.implied_outcome: At least one U.S. state formally adopts a pause by January 31, 2027. The reported support from some Republican governors and reported implementation of moratoriums by state representatives imply a near-term path to at least one adoption, though no state or adoption date is specified.

article:
Tom Lee Says Nvidia Just Broke Wall Street's Most Unusual Pattern
Nvidia (NVDA) jumped 8.74% on August 27 after a record quarter. Fundstrat's Tom Lee says the chipmaker almost never rises on good earnings.
Lee calls the reaction proof that the market is healthy. However, the gains only lasted one day, and Nvidia fell 4.57% on Friday to $217.55.
Nvidia has beaten Wall Street estimates for years. The stock still fell after each of its last four reports. It went into this one cold, and shares slid seven sessions in a row from August 14 to August 24, dropping from $225.30 to $208.48.
Then the numbers landed, and Nvidia's post-earnings reversal carried the stock to $227.98, adding roughly $440 billion in market value in one day.
The quarter was not close. Revenue hit $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year ago. Nvidia guided the current quarter to $108 billion.
Lee thinks it was a funding problem. Investors who owned too little Nvidia had to sell something else to buy it.
Software went the other way, with Salesforce climbing 22.58% on its own results, and effectively becoming one of several stocks that outgained Nvidia that day.
Lee also pointed at the price-to-earnings (PE) ratio. Nvidia trades at 27.5 times past earnings, but only 18 times expected earnings. Estimates are climbing faster than the stock.
"The thing that stands out is Nvidia's multiple is still very low. So, they've got these huge revisions. The stock hasn't kept up. Now the PE keeps contracting," Tom Lee, Fundstrat managing partner and head of research, speaking on CNBC.
However, not everyone is convinced. Jay Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners holds the only sell rating on the stock. He argues the sold-out supply constraint caps the upside, because Nvidia cannot ship chips it has already promised.
Lee flagged one more risk. Opposition to new data centers is turning into an election issue, and some Republican governors now back a pause.
The pattern broke on Thursday. By Friday it had closed again, with about $250 billion of the gain gone.
